A new article in the Lancet (8 November 2021) provides a peer-reviewed chronological analysis of crucial junctures and international obligations in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What happened day by day, where, why, or why not?

The information was gathered by the Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response. The Panel was co-chaired by former New Zealand Prime Minister the Rt Hon. Helen Clark, and Her Excellency Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, former President of Liberia.

Before COVID-19, most societies treated large-scale infectious disease as a contingency rather than a daily organizing principle, while work, schooling, healthcare, shopping, travel, and social life were predominantly in-person and digital services were usually supplements rather than substitutes. The first decisive break came in late 2019 and early 2020, when the World Health Organization received reports of unexplained pneumonia in Wuhan on 31 December 2019, Wuhan imposed strict measures on 23 January, the WHO declared an international public-health emergency on 30 January, and the WHO formally described COVID-19 as a pandemic on 11 March. The initial response transformed ordinary mobility into a public-health variable: Wuhan suspended public transport and blocked departure from the city, Italy imposed the first national lockdown outside China, U.S. states closed schools and non-essential businesses, and by April 2020 roughly 3.9 billion people in more than 90 countries or territories had been asked or ordered to stay home. Public health consequently moved from the background to the centre of government, workplaces, and personal decision-making, with masks, distancing, testing, ventilation, contact tracing, quarantine, and capacity limits becoming routine features of life that had scarcely existed for most people before 2020. [shard_01319_69111] [shard_04577_38493]

The emergency exposed weaknesses that had been obscured by normal conditions, including shortages of intensive-care beds, protective equipment, ventilators, personnel, and testing capacity, while delayed diagnosis and treatment for non-COVID illnesses contributed to excess deaths beyond those directly attributed to the virus. [shard_04577_38493]

The scale was simultaneously medical and economic: by December 2021 more than 285 million cases and 5.4 million deaths had been reported, global economic growth was estimated to have fallen by 3.2 percent in 2020, trade by 5.3 percent, and roughly 75 million people had entered extreme poverty.
